clue.text: "Algernon was in the hearts of women" (Meredith, Rhoda Fleming)

definitions.text: "Algernon was in the hearts of women" (Meredith, Rhoda Fleming)

parts.words: "Algernon was in the hearts of women" (Meredith, Rhoda Fleming)
parts.note: a quotation with a word missing between 'was' and 'in': the solver supplies the word Meredith wrote in his novel Rhoda Fleming

explanation.surface: A line from Meredith about a young man who has made no impression on women.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank clue: the gap after 'was' is lost in the print, and the missing word means not yet read, nobody having looked into Algernon.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation needs a word meaning that Algernon remained a closed book, never perused by women's hearts.

clue.text: He offered 5 Down (syndicated it for new edition)

definitions.text: He offered 5 Down (syndicated it for new edition)

parts.words: He offered 5 Down (syndicated it for new edition)
parts.note: the man who wrote the novel at 5 Down; the bracket shows the title as letters of 'syndicated it for' in a new edition, that is, rearranged

explanation.surface: A publisher offered a feature and syndicated it for a fresh edition.
explanation.walkthrough: With 4 Down this gives the full name of the author of the 1955 satire Cards of Identity; the letters of 'syndicated it for' rearrange to that title, a clue within the clue. This light holds the first name only.
explanation.definitionFit: The writer Nigel Dennis published the novel Cards of Identity, the answer to 5 Down.

clue.text: One of Elizabeth Bowen's meetings

parts.note: Bowen's first story collection (1923) has a plural title meaning meetings; one of them is the singular word

explanation.surface: One of the gatherings the novelist Elizabeth Bowen attended.
explanation.walkthrough: Elizabeth Bowen's debut collection of stories was called Encounters, so 'one of' her meetings is the singular.
explanation.definitionFit: A chance meeting with someone is a common synonym, here also echoing a book title.

clue.text: See

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'See (6)': a cross-reference to 2-down (NIGEL DENNIS) with no group linking the two lights in the puzzle file, so there is no clue text of its own to annotate.

clue.text: Hero of Howell's work discovers mountain pass to French town

parts.note: a col is a pass between mountain peaks
ville is the French word for town

explanation.surface: The hero of a novel finds a route over the mountains into a town in France.
explanation.walkthrough: Theodore Colville is the hero of W. D. Howells's novel Indian Summer.
explanation.definitionFit: Theodore Colville is the protagonist of Howells's novel Indian Summer, set in Florence.

clue.text: They proved we were somebody in wartime

definitions.text: They proved we were somebody in wartime

parts.words: They proved we were somebody in wartime
parts.note: documents every Briton carried during the Second World War to prove who they were

explanation.surface: Wartime memories of feeling that one counted for something.
explanation.walkthrough: Britain issued compulsory identity documents from 1939 to 1952; it is also the title of Nigel Dennis's novel (2 and 4 Down).
explanation.definitionFit: Official papers showing a holder's name proved who that person was, hence that they were 'somebody'.

clue.text: Securely close seat of affection, say, for one who attacked the "Cockney School of Poetry"

definitions.text: one who attacked the "Cockney School of Poetry"

parts.note: to lock is to fasten securely

indicators.note: say signals that the word is to be heard rather than spelt as written

parts.note: the heart is traditionally where love resides

explanation.surface: Fastening something tight, with a romantic aside, in praise of a critic who mocked Keats and Hunt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' turns HEART into its sound-alike HART. J. G. Lockhart attacked Keats, Leigh Hunt and their circle as the 'Cockney School' in Blackwood's Magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: John Gibson Lockhart wrote the Blackwood's essays deriding the 'Cockney School of Poetry'.

clue.text: Embrace beginnings of Italy's new art renaissance movement

indicators.note: beginnings of tells us to take only the opening letter of each of the five words that follow

explanation.surface: Italy welcomes a new artistic revival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginnings of' takes the initials of Italy's, new, art, renaissance and movement.
explanation.definitionFit: To inarm is an old verb for clasping someone in one's arms, a literary synonym.

clue.text: Walter de la Mare's audience

parts.note: de la Mare's best-known poem is named after the ghostly hearers who attend to the Traveller's knock

explanation.surface: The people who came to hear the poet Walter de la Mare.
explanation.walkthrough: In de la Mare's poem The Listeners, a Traveller knocks at a moonlit door heard only by phantom auditors.
explanation.definitionFit: An audience is made up of people hearing something, and de la Mare's poem is titled after them.

clue.text: Seems to define emperor's utterance, ascribed on Graves's book

definitions.text: Seems to define emperor's utterance, ascribed on Graves's book

parts.words: Seems to define emperor's utterance, ascribed on Graves's book
parts.note: Graves's novel I, Claudius opens its title with the emperor saying 'I', which looks self-centred

explanation.surface: A remark by an emperor, quoted on the cover of a Robert Graves novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The emperor's utterance is 'I', the first word of the title I, Claudius; a book that starts with 'I' seems all about the self.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone self-absorbed puts 'I' first, as the title of Graves's novel does.

clue.text: It interrupted Papa's sunrises

parts.note: Papa is Hemingway's nickname; his novel's title puts a short word between 'Sun' and 'Rises'

explanation.surface: Something broke into a father's dawn routine.
explanation.walkthrough: Hemingway, known as Papa, wrote The Sun Also Rises: the third word sits between Sun and Rises.
explanation.definitionFit: The word in the middle of Hemingway's title, meaning in addition, splits 'sun' from 'rises'.

clue.text: Marion Crawford's Swedish doctor recalls Danish fratricide

definitions.meaning: Dr ... (1883) is a novel by F. Marion Crawford about a Swedish scholar
in Hamlet the King of Denmark murdered his brother, old Hamlet

explanation.surface: A novelist's Swedish physician brings to mind a Danish brother-killer.
explanation.definitionFit: The same name serves Crawford's title character and Hamlet's uncle, who poisoned his brother the king.

clue.text: Instrument of percussive engineering introduced by Spillane

definitions.meaning: a tool used for striking nails and metal
Mickey Spillane created the private eye Mike ...

explanation.surface: Mickey Spillane brings in a noisy industrial tool.
explanation.definitionFit: The striking tool shares its name with the detective Mike Hammer, whom Spillane first brought on in I, the Jury.

clue.text: "As it —, it ain't, thats logic" (Lewis Carroll)

definitions.text: "As it —, it ain't, thats logic" (Lewis Carroll)

parts.words: "As it —, it ain't, thats logic" (Lewis Carroll)
parts.note: Tweedledee's speech in Through the Looking-Glass with one word blanked by the dash

explanation.surface: A line of Tweedledee's mock reasoning from Carroll.
explanation.walkthrough: Tweedledee says: 'if it was so, it might be; and if it were so, it would be; but as it isn't, it ain't. That's logic.'
explanation.definitionFit: The gap needs the negative contraction of 'is not' that Tweedledee uses.

clue.text: A number noticed around occurrence by Tarkington

indicators.note: around tells us the word for noticed is wrapped about the word for occurrence

parts.note: something noticed has been seen
an event is something that occurs

explanation.surface: A figure observed close to some happening in a Booth Tarkington book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by Tarkington' is not wordplay: Booth Tarkington wrote the novel Seventeen (1916), so it points to the answer as a book title, beside the plain definition 'A number'.
explanation.definitionFit: Seventeen is a whole number, and the title of a Tarkington novel.

clue.text: Woodsman who chronicled hearts of oak

definitions.meaning: a person who looks after a forest
C. S. ... wrote the Hornblower novels of Nelson's navy, whose men were the 'hearts of oak' of the song

explanation.surface: A man of the woods who wrote the history of oak trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart of Oak' is the Royal Navy's march, so 'hearts of oak' are sailors, not trees.
explanation.definitionFit: A forest worker shares the surname of C. S. Forester, author of naval novels.

clue.text: He claimed to be the equal of Zeus, but his daughter was a mere tyro

definitions.text: He claimed to be the equal of Zeus, but his daughter was a mere tyro

parts.words: He claimed to be the equal of Zeus, but his daughter was a mere tyro
parts.note: a Greek king who mimicked Zeus's thunder and was struck down; his daughter was named Tyro, which also means a beginner

explanation.surface: A boastful father whose daughter was only a novice.
explanation.walkthrough: Salmoneus of Elis drove a chariot to imitate thunder and was killed by Zeus's bolt; his daughter Tyro bore Neleus and Pelias to Poseidon.
explanation.definitionFit: Salmoneus is the mythical king who set himself up as Zeus's rival, father of Tyro.

clue.text: City Giraudoux associated with bad moods

definitions.text: City Giraudoux associated with bad moods

parts.words: City Giraudoux associated with bad moods
parts.note: 'bad moods' rearranged gives the first, so the clue wants the other

explanation.surface: A town the dramatist linked with ill temper.
explanation.walkthrough: MOODS rearranged gives SODOM, and Giraudoux named his 1943 play Sodome et Gomorrhe, so the city wanted is the partner in the title, in its French spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Gomorrah, spelt the French way, is the city paired with Sodom in Giraudoux's play title.

clue.text: Somewhat too much from Arthur Hailey

definitions.meaning: an excess load, more than can be carried
Hailey's 1979 novel about a power company is titled ...

explanation.surface: Arthur Hailey writing a little more than needed.
explanation.definitionFit: An excessive burden is too much, and Hailey's power-crisis novel bears the same title.

clue.text: Like Mary Shelley's man, (or was it Alfred Noyes's?)

definitions.text: Like Mary Shelley's man, (or was it Alfred Noyes's?)

parts.words: Like Mary Shelley's man, (or was it Alfred Noyes's?)
parts.note: Mary Shelley's 1826 novel about the sole survivor of a plague, and Noyes's 1940 novel, share a title describing such a man

explanation.surface: A writer unsure whether a character belongs to Mary Shelley or Alfred Noyes.
explanation.walkthrough: Both Mary Shelley (1826) and Alfred Noyes (1940) wrote a novel called The Last Man.
explanation.definitionFit: Both books describe a final survivor, the man left at the end of humanity.

clue.text: Shakespearean knight uses small caps, gets poor return

parts.note: s.c. is the printer's abbreviation for small capitals

indicators.note: return tells us the word poor is to be read backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A knight from Shakespeare uses small capitals in print and gets meagre profit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns POOR into ROOP. Sir Stephen Scroop appears in Richard II; Lord Scroop is a traitor in Henry V.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Stephen Scroop is a knight loyal to the king in Shakespeare's Richard II.

clue.text: Italian composer suggested by model in Indian costume

indicators.note: in tells us the model letter is placed inside the costume

parts.note: a sari is the draped garment worn by Indian women
the Model T was Ford's famous car, so model gives T

explanation.surface: An Italian composer brought to mind by a model wearing Indian dress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts T, from Ford's Model T, inside SARI. Giuseppe Sarti (1729-1802) was an Italian opera composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Sarti was an eighteenth-century Italian composer of opera.

clue.text: He conducted a dance to the music of time

definitions.text: He conducted a dance to the music of time

parts.words: He conducted a dance to the music of time
parts.note: Anthony Powell's twelve-novel sequence A Dance to the Music of Time is narrated by Nick Jenkins

explanation.surface: A bandleader who led dancers in time with the music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conducted' suggests a bandleader, but here it means guided the reader: Nicholas Jenkins narrates Powell's sequence.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas Jenkins is the narrator who leads readers through Powell's novel cycle.

clue.text: Clifford Odets and Ernest Lehman associated it with success

definitions.text: Clifford Odets and Ernest Lehman associated it with success

parts.words: Clifford Odets and Ernest Lehman associated it with success
parts.note: the two wrote the screenplay of Sweet Smell of Success (1957); the clue wants a word for a smell

explanation.surface: Two screenwriters connecting something with achievement.
explanation.walkthrough: Odets and Lehman wrote the film Sweet Smell of Success; a sweet smell is a pleasant scent.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleasant scent, the sweet smell the film title links with success.

clue.text: Helen Cresswell's psychiatrist apparently expensive

definitions.meaning: Helen Cresswell's novel ... Shrink is about children writing to a psychiatrist

explanation.surface: A children's author's analyst, it seems, charges a lot.
explanation.walkthrough: A psychiatrist is a 'shrink', and Cresswell's book Dear Shrink addresses one in the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Costly goods are called dear in Britain, and a letter to a shrink opens with the same word.

clue.text: Heavy piece by Ionesco, now endangered

definitions.meaning: Ionesco's absurdist play about townsfolk turning into a large horned beast
most species of this horned animal are now threatened with extinction

explanation.surface: A weighty play by Ionesco is now at risk.
explanation.definitionFit: Ionesco's 1959 play shares its title with a massive horned animal now threatened in the wild.

clue.text: Improbable as Gray's stories, mostly SWORD

definitions.meaning: Alasdair Gray's 1983 collection is titled ... Stories, Mostly

explanation.surface: Alasdair Gray's tales are mostly hard to believe.
explanation.walkthrough: The trailing 'SWORD' is OCR debris where the letter count was printed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something improbable is not to be expected, the word Gray used for his collection title.

clue.text: Some pressure applied to provincial letter writer 2&4 He offered (syndicated it for new edition)

definitions.meaning: Blaise ... wrote the Lettres provinciales (Provincial Letters)

explanation.surface: Pressure being put on a country correspondent.
explanation.walkthrough: The held clue has the 2 and 4 Down clue run into its end by the OCR; only the words before it belong here.
explanation.definitionFit: The SI unit of pressure is named after Blaise Pascal, author of the Provincial Letters.
